takeaway: A human hand packs about 20 ways to move and dense touch into a small space; most robots use a simple two-finger clamp instead and lose most of that.

selfCheck.question: Why do so many robots still use a two-finger clamp?
selfCheck.answer: much simpler: one motor instead of 16, no fingertip sensors; cheaper, less likely to break, easier to control; most of the time only pick and place; falls short when the object must be turned in the grip.

sentence: A simple robot clamp uses one motor to open and close two fingers. A human-like robot hand needs many joints, each with its own motor, and touch sensors as well, which makes it much harder to build. What you get for that effort is a hand that can move and turn an object while holding it, which a clamp cannot do.

"8.3 million tiny touch-sensing spots" (what a spot is)

reason: My takeaway was about how hard robot hands are to build (16 motors and sensors against one motor) and what a hand can do in return, but it left out the human hand's roughly 20 movements and dense touch, the small space they fit into, and the fact that most robots use a clamp and lose most of that.
